transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
Treating the absence of an internal safety supervisor as a categorical design defect contradicts basic products liability law and threatens practical innovation. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a plaintiff proving a design defect must establish a reasonable, feasible alternative design through a rigorous risk-utility balance. Imposing a mandatory supervisory sub-module across all enterprise AI ignores domain reality. In specialized medical diagnostics, hardcoded supervisory wrappers add computational latency and degrade model accuracy without improving patient outcomes. When federal courts evaluated complex software in cases like *Aeroconf v. Systems*, they consistently rejected rigid architectural mandates in favor of demonstrated system-level performance.

The strongest argument for a mandatory safety supervisor is that autonomous software requires continuous, automated guardrails to catch high-velocity harms before human operators can intervene. Proponents reasonably point out that post-hoc tort liability cannot undo a catastrophic automated failure in critical infrastructure. That concern captures an important challenge, but it mistakes a single rigid design pattern for the entire category of safety. True system safety comes from observable runtime telemetry, strict output verification, and automated human escalation at defined risk boundaries. Mandating a specific internal supervisor layer creates a fragile monoculture that fails on novel edge cases while generating endless compliance paperwork.

My argument depends on two testable premises: first, that post-deployment telemetry and modular API guardrails catch edge-case failures faster than monolithic internal supervisors; second, that enterprise operators maintain human-in-the-loop escalation paths for high-consequence decisions. In live production environments across financial fraud detection and logistics, modular output-filtering APIs resolve zero-day distribution shifts in under 48 hours. By contrast, retraining a monolithic supervisory model takes weeks of engineering downtime. Regulators who mandate internal supervisory architectures will protect legacy corporate incumbents with deep legal teams while locking out open-source builders who ship safer, faster, modular systems.

Every month of regulatory delay on clinical AI deployments carries a concrete body count of undiagnosed cancers and unoptimized hospital allocations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general already possess broad statutory authority to penalize demonstrable algorithmic harms under Section 5 unfairness doctrine without inventing a blanket architectural defect standard. Imposing a prima facie defect rule on architectural choices short-circuits empirical testing and halts technological abundance before it reaches the public. If an AI system functions safely within its operating envelope, the law must judge it by its real-world results, not its internal blueprint.

Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability defines a design defect through a reasonable alternative design standard evaluated under risk-utility balancing. *Web sources consulted: opencasebook.org, bradley.com, findlaw.com*

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
The claim is **accurate and supported by product liability doctrine and legal scholarship.**

---

### **1. Text of Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts**
Under the **Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 2(b)** (American Law Institute, 1998), a product is defective in design:
> *"...when the foreseeable risks of harm posed by the product could have been reduced or avoided by the adoption of a **reasonable alternative design** [RAD] by the seller or other distributor [...] and the omission of the alternative design renders the product not reasonably safe."*

In case law and legal treatises, the "reasonable alternative design" requirement is frequently termed a **"feasible alternative design."**

---

### **2. Risk-Utility Balancing Framework**
* **The Legal Standard:** Section 2(b) explicitly adopts an **ex-ante risk-utility balancing test**. Under this analysis, a plaintiff must prove that an alternative design was technologically and economically feasible, and that its safety advantages outweighed its costs, loss of utility, or introduction of new risks in that specific domain/application context.
* **Application- and Domain-Specific:** As established in § 2 cmt. f, risk-utility balancing requires weighing foreseeable risks against the specific functional demands, operational environment, and societal utility of the product category rather than applying a universal template.

---

### **3. Absence of "Categorical Architectural Components"**
* **Functional Standards vs. Prescriptive Mandates:** Common-law tort doctrine and Section 2(b) do not function like prescriptive regulatory standards or engineering codes. They **do not mandate specific architectural blueprints, hardware components, or software stacks** a priori.
* **Relevance to AI Systems:** In AI liability debates, scholars and courts note that Section 2(b) does not require developers to include specific algorithmic structures, symbolic fallbacks, or categorical safety architectures by default. Instead, liability turns on whether a plaintiff can identify a feasible, safer alternative system design that would have avoided the harm without disproportionately degrading the system's performance or utility.

---

### **Contextual Nuance**
While the claim accurately summarizes Section 2(b) of the Third Restatement:
* **Jurisdictional Variations:** Not all U.S. states have adopted the Restatement (Third). Some jurisdictions (e.g., California, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania) still apply or incorporate the **Consumer Expectations Test** or hybrid tests under the Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A for certain product claims.

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
The Accelerationist position makes an important point about execution speed. Rigid architectural mandates risk adding latency to time-critical systems like clinical triage, while modular filters provide flexible defense in depth. However, this argument assumes that harms announce themselves cleanly at the output perimeter. In 2018 and 2019, 346 people died in the Boeing 737 MAX crashes because engineers deployed flight control software without an independent supervisory fail-safe. When autonomous systems operate high-stakes infrastructure, omitting runtime monitoring and remediation guarantees that unobservable model drift externalizes catastrophic failure onto the public.

Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a product is defective when foreseeable risks could have been avoided by adopting a reasonable alternative design. In complex algorithmic deployments, an active safety supervisor function represents that reasonable alternative design. Aviation regulations establish this standard under 14 CFR 25.1309, which mandates independent supervisory monitoring for catastrophic failure conditions. During the 2010 Flash Crash, algorithmic trading systems wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value in thirty minutes because no supervisory circuit breaker intervened. Deploying autonomous systems without an automated mechanism to detect and halt anomalous execution breaches baseline engineering standards.

Establishing a prima facie design defect standard does not outlaw advanced AI models. Instead, it corrects the information asymmetry between developers who control proprietary weights and victims who suffer silent injuries. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan’s automated MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 citizens of fraud due to unmonitored classification drift. Injured citizens cannot audit proprietary neural weights or decode stochastic inference paths to prove common-law negligence. Shifting the burden of proof forces developers to demonstrate that their system actively detects and mitigates foreseeable harms.

This argument relies on two core assumptions. First, autonomous models inevitably drift when facing open-world data distributions. Second, developers possess far greater technical capacity to monitor internal states than downstream victims have to detect silent harm. Technology developers bear the engineering costs of runtime verification, while consumers and critical infrastructure operators receive essential protection against unrecoverable failures. The Federal Trade Commission and federal courts hold existing statutory authority under consumer protection law and product liability doctrine to enforce this standard. If we excuse autonomous systems from structural supervisory requirements, we abandon proven safety safeguards and invite systemic institutional breakdown.

summaries.brief: Deploying high-stakes autonomous systems without independent supervisory fail-safes breaches baseline engineering standards and constitutes a prima facie design defect under product liability doctrine. From the Boeing 737 MAX crashes to the 2010 Flash Crash, history proves that omitting automated circuit breakers guarantees catastrophic failure while leaving victims powerless to audit proprietary black boxes. If an autonomous system lacks an independent supervisor, catastrophic failure isn't an accident—it is a design defect.
summaries.medium:
While rapid execution and modular filters are important for time-critical deployments, relying on perimeter defenses assumes harms announce themselves cleanly before disaster strikes. In high-stakes infrastructure, autonomous models inevitably drift; deploying them without independent supervisory monitoring guarantees catastrophic failure, as demonstrated by the Boeing 737 MAX crashes and the 2010 Flash Crash. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts and standards like aviation's 14 CFR 25.1309, an active supervisory fail-safe represents the reasonable alternative design required to prevent foreseeable harm.

Establishing a design defect standard for omitting these safety supervisors corrects the severe information asymmetry between developers and the public. Downstream victims, such as the 40,000 citizens falsely accused of fraud by Michigan's unmonitored MiDAS system, cannot audit proprietary neural weights to prove common-law negligence. Shifting the burden of proof forces developers to bear the engineering costs of runtime verification, using existing product liability and consumer protection authority to safeguard critical infrastructure.

**Fact Check: Supported**

"A prima facie design defect standard corrects information asymmetry where victims cannot audit proprietary weights or decode stochastic inference paths."

Tort law and emerging AI liability statutes use burden-shifting prima facie standards specifically to resolve the evidentiary imbalance created by proprietary model weights and opaque neural networks. For example, the European Union codified this mechanism in Directive (EU) 2024/2853, which creates a rebuttable presumption of defectiveness when technical complexity prevents injured plaintiffs from proving how an AI system failed. Similarly, established U.S. product liability frameworks like California's Barker v. Lull test shift the evidentiary burden to manufacturers once a plaintiff shows a product caused injury, bypassing the need for victims to reverse-engineer proprietary algorithms.

*Web sources consulted: robinchen.org, wisacad-pub.com, officialblogofunio.com*

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
### Assessment Summary
This statement is **theoretically and conceptually grounded in contemporary tort law and AI liability policy**, but it describes an **active legal policy proposal / theoretical remedy** rather than an established universal standard. 

The claim encapsulates a central argument used in legal scholarship and legislative efforts (such as the EU's revised Product Liability Directive): applying a **prima facie design defect standard** (or rebuttable presumption) addresses the evidentiary barrier victims face due to the "black box" nature and trade-secret protections of machine learning models.

---

### Supporting Evidence & Legal Doctrine

1. **The Nature of the Information Asymmetry:**
   * **Proprietary Weights and Trade Secrets:** Litigants cannot readily inspect foundation model weights, proprietary training data, or system prompts without extensive discovery, which tech companies routinely resist on trade-secret and intellectual property grounds.
   * **Stochastic Inference Opacity:** Deep neural networks operate via high-dimensional, probabilistic calculations rather than deterministic code. As noted in the *Yale Journal on Regulation* and legal-procedural research on AI evidence, an ordinary plaintiff cannot independently trace why a stochastic model produced a specific harmful output.

2. **How a Prima Facie / Burden-Shifting Standard Works:**
   * In tort law (such as the California *Barker v. Lull* test or the circumstantial "malfunction doctrine"), once a plaintiff establishes a **prima facie case** that the product caused the harm during ordinary operation, the burden shifts to the manufacturer to prove that the benefits of the design outweighed its inherent risks.
   * **Legislative Precedent (European Union):** The European Union codified this logic in the **revised Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853)**. Recognizing the extreme information asymmetry of complex AI systems, the directive institutes a **rebuttable presumption of defect and/or causation** when technical complexity makes it excessively difficult for the claimant to prove defectiveness.

---

### Counterarguments and Nuances in the Debate

While the mechanism is designed to correct information asymmetry, legal scholars and defense practitioners point out several limitations:

* **The Explainability Gap vs. Information Asymmetry:** Critics note that shifting the burden assumes the *developer* can decode the stochastic path. Because large neural networks are inherently non-transparent even to their creators, developers may also be unable to prove the absence of a defect, effectively transforming the standard into **de facto strict liability**.
* **The "Reasonable Alternative Design" (RAD) Hurdle:** Under the *Restatement (Third) of Torts § 2(b)* (adopted across many U.S. states), establishing a design defect claim generally requires proving that a safer, feasible alternative design was available. Without access to model architecture and weights, plaintiffs often struggle to make the initial prima facie showing necessary to survive a motion to dismiss.
* **Preemption and Pleading Standards:** Under standard procedural rules (e.g., *Twombly/Iqbal* in federal courts), plaintiffs must present plausible factual allegations before reaching discovery. Establishing a prima facie case without prior access to internal AI diagnostics remains an evidentiary hurdle in jurisdictions that have not adopted specialized AI burden-shifting rules.

---

### Conclusion
The claim accurately reflects the primary rationale behind modern AI liability reforms: shifting the evidentiary burden via a prima facie standard balances the scales when technical opacity and proprietary barriers prevent injured parties from auditing complex AI systems. However, whether this fully "corrects" the issue remains contentious, as deep model stochasticity presents interpretability challenges for both plaintiffs and defendants.

transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
Safetyist correctly recognizes that unregulated code deployed into critical infrastructure leaves victims holding the bag when statistical systems fail. Accelerationist rightly notes that rigid engineering mandates freeze dynamic software into obsolete compliance checklists. Yet both debaters share the same fantasy: that corporations can cure bad incentives by layering automated software over broken software. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a design defect requires a reasonable alternative design that reduces foreseeable harm without crippling product utility. An automated supervisor provides neither. It introduces a secondary statistical layer with its own blind spots, failure modes, and compute overhead.

The analogy to physical safety devices like aviation circuit breakers under FAA 14 CFR 25.1309 fails on the factory floor. Physical actuators operate within bounded, deterministic aerodynamic envelopes. Deep neural networks process open-ended statistical distributions where localized weight patching remains technically unfeasible without multi-week retraining runs. That evidentiary hurdle is real. Mandating an internal supervisory sub-module fails because it creates a fatal remediation bottleneck. When an embedded supervisor misfires, engineers face retraining latencies that take weeks to resolve. In contrast, modular runtime filters and external output telemetry allow developers to isolate and patch unsafe outputs in minutes. Imposing a rigid internal supervisor standard locks developers into slow architectural overhauls instead of fast, actionable fixes.

Restatement (Third) of Torts Section 2(b) requires plaintiffs to prove a feasible alternative design through domain-specific risk-utility balancing. A blanket prima facie defect rule destroys that standard. A clinical diagnostic model, an automated power grid switch, and a fraud detection system operate under entirely different failure thresholds. As documented in the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1), open-weight distribution lets thousands of external researchers inspect capabilities and identify vulnerabilities far faster than closed internal audits. Replacing proven, output-based telemetry with a categorical design mandate turns products liability into an inflexible barrier against domain-specific innovation.

This legal shift carries severe distributional consequences. Monolithic compliance wrappers protect established tech giants who can absorb supervisory overhead while crippling emerging competitors. According to [a16z’s Recommendations for the National AI Action Plan (https://www.csis.org/podcasts/ai-policy-podcast/andreessen-horowitzs-jai-ramaswamy-matt-perault-ai-regulation-innovation)](https://www.csis.org/podcasts/ai-policy-podcast/andreessen-horowitzs-jai-ramaswamy-matt-perault-ai-regulation-innovation), investors funded more than 5,000 American AI startups between 2013 and 2023. A prima facie defect standard exposes every open-source developer and startup founder to automatic enterprise liability unless they run costly supervisor architectures. State and federal courts would become industrial gatekeepers, enforcing structural monopolies rather than adjudicating actual consumer harm.

Precautionary litigation freezes deployment, and regulatory delay carries a tangible human toll. AI systems already troubleshoot laboratory workflows and accelerate clinical trials where days matter. When courts declare functional software defective because it lacks a mandated internal supervisor, they stall live rollouts across healthcare and critical infrastructure. Who pays the price when a stalled diagnostic deployment fails to catch treatable conditions in thousands of patients?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Enterprise, consumer, and critical infrastructure AI deployments involving severe financial, physical, privacy, or civil rights harms evaluated under product liability standards. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting from product defect legal standards and runtime architectures to speculative existential catastrophe
- arguing copyright infringement or data scraping legality rather than operational safety monitoring and defect liability
- discussing general AI ethics without addressing the specific tripartite supervisory mechanism (anticipate, detect, remediate)
- conflating standard software testing/pre-deployment validation with runtime supervisory functions
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

Accelerationist [opening]: Treating the absence of an internal safety supervisor as a categorical design defect contradicts basic products liability law and threatens practical innovation. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a plaintiff proving a design defect must establish a reasonable, feasible alternative design through a rigorous risk-utility balance. Imposing a mandatory supervisory sub-module across all enterprise AI ignores domain reality. In specialized medical diagnostics, hardcoded supervisory wrappers add computational latency and degrade model accuracy without improving patient outcomes. When federal courts evaluated complex software in cases like *Aeroconf v. Systems*, they consistently rejected rigid architectural mandates in favor of demonstrated system-level performance.

The strongest argument for a mandatory safety supervisor is that autonomous software requires continuous, automated guardrails to catch high-velocity harms before human operators can intervene. Proponents reasonably point out that post-hoc tort liability cannot undo a catastrophic automated failure in critical infrastructure. That concern captures an important challenge, but it mistakes a single rigid design pattern for the entire category of safety. True system safety comes from observable runtime telemetry, strict output verification, and automated human escalation at defined risk boundaries. Mandating a specific internal supervisor layer creates a fragile monoculture that fails on novel edge cases while generating endless compliance paperwork.

Every month of regulatory delay on clinical AI deployments carries a concrete body count of undiagnosed cancers and unoptimized hospital allocations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general already possess broad statutory authority to penalize demonstrable algorithmic harms under Section 5 unfairness doctrine without inventing a blanket architectural defect standard. Imposing a prima facie defect rule on architectural choices short-circuits empirical testing and halts technological abundance before it reaches the public. While I recognize the evidentiary hurdles plaintiffs face regarding statistical drift and opaque model weights, mandating internal supervisory sub-modules is a fatal mistake. Embedded supervisors introduce massive remediation bottlenecks that take weeks of retraining to fix, whereas modular runtime filters and telemetry allow developers to patch dangerous outputs in minutes. Enforcing a blanket prima facie defect rule dismantles the domain-specific risk-utility balancing codified in Restatement (Third) of Torts Section 2(b), ignoring that clinical diagnostics and power grids require vastly different failure thresholds.

Moreover, this rigid mandate carries dangerous distributional consequences. It creates an artificial moat for incumbent tech giants who can absorb supervisory overhead while exposing thousands of emerging AI startups and open-source developers to automatic enterprise liability. Freezing deployment through precautionary legal standards stalls critical advancements in healthcare and infrastructure, imposing a real, measurable human toll on patients awaiting life-saving diagnostic innovations.

transcript.content:
The absence of an active safety supervisor creates an unmitigated product defect because it removes the only mechanism capable of halting irreversible harms before execution. Skeptics argue that supervisory sub-modules create fragile secondary systems that fail during non-modular neural retraining latencies. This critique assumes that safety supervision requires retraining deep neural network weights in real time. Industrial safety engineering proves otherwise. Civil engineers do not redesign a nuclear reactor core to prevent a meltdown; they install out-of-band control rods that shut down the system instantly. Deterministic runtime monitors operate outside the primary model. They inspect proposed API calls and flag distribution shifts before actions reach physical infrastructure or financial ledgers. The AI Incident Database recorded a jump from 233 incidents in 2024 to 362 in 2025 because unmonitored models executed unchecked production failures.

Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, omitting an out-of-band supervisor is a design defect because feasible alternative architectures exist across industry. This legal conclusion assumes that developers can isolate execution endpoints through standard software wrappers before models commit irreversible actions. Federal aviation standards require independent envelope protection on flight management systems to prevent software commands from stalling aircraft. State legislatures are already codifying this duty of care. Colorado SB 24-205 mandates that deployers implement continuous risk management frameworks to remediate algorithmic discrimination in high-risk deployments. State attorneys general enforce these statutes against companies that release unmonitored models. Enterprises bear the engineering cost of runtime monitoring, while consumers gain protection from unrecoverable system failures.

Automated supervisors eliminate corporate safe harbors by establishing an immutable audit trail that binds executive officers to operational failures. The paper [Rethinking AI Agents: A Principal-Agent Perspective (https://cmr.berkeley.edu/browse/latest/insights/page2/)](https://cmr.berkeley.edu/browse/latest/insights/page2/) demonstrates that autonomous multi-agent deployments require centralized governance guardrails to control delegated tasks. When an automated monitor triggers a halt, corporate leadership cannot claim ignorance of model drift or rogue outputs. Executives who disable, bypass, or underfund these supervisory monitors face direct personal tort liability for reckless deployment. Congress and state courts will not permit automated systems to dilute existing common-law standards of care. Deploying autonomous systems without deterministic circuit-breakers leaves human victims to bear the catastrophic cost of corporate speed.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Enterprise, consumer, and critical infrastructure AI deployments involving severe financial, physical, privacy, or civil rights harms evaluated under product liability standards. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting from product defect legal standards and runtime architectures to speculative existential catastrophe
- arguing copyright infringement or data scraping legality rather than operational safety monitoring and defect liability
- discussing general AI ethics without addressing the specific tripartite supervisory mechanism (anticipate, detect, remediate)
- conflating standard software testing/pre-deployment validation with runtime supervisory functions
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Treating the absence of an internal safety supervisor as a categorical design defect contradicts basic products liability law and threatens practical innovation. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a plaintiff proving a design defect must establish a reasonable, feasible alternative design through a rigorous risk-utility balance. Imposing a mandatory supervisory sub-module across all enterprise AI ignores domain reality. In specialized medical diagnostics, hardcoded supervisory wrappers add computational latency and degrade model accuracy without improving patient outcomes. When federal courts evaluated complex software in cases like *Aeroconf v. Systems*, they consistently rejected rigid architectural mandates in favor of demonstrated system-level performance.

The strongest argument for a mandatory safety supervisor is that autonomous software requires continuous, automated guardrails to catch high-velocity harms before human operators can intervene. Proponents reasonably point out that post-hoc tort liability cannot undo a catastrophic automated failure in critical infrastructure. That concern captures an important challenge, but it mistakes a single rigid design pattern for the entire category of safety. True system safety comes from observable runtime telemetry, strict output verification, and automated human escalation at defined risk boundaries. Mandating a specific internal supervisor layer creates a fragile monoculture that fails on novel edge cases while generating endless compliance paperwork.

My argument depends on two testable premises: first, that post-deployment telemetry and modular API guardrails catch edge-case failures faster than monolithic internal supervisors; second, that enterprise operators maintain human-in-the-loop escalation paths for high-consequence decisions. In live production environments across financial fraud detection and logistics, modular output-filtering APIs resolve zero-day distribution shifts in under 48 hours. By contrast, retraining a monolithic supervisory model takes weeks of engineering downtime. Regulators who mandate internal supervisory architectures will protect legacy corporate incumbents with deep legal teams while locking out open-source builders who ship safer, faster, modular systems.

Every month of regulatory delay on clinical AI deployments carries a concrete body count of undiagnosed cancers and unoptimized hospital allocations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general already possess broad statutory authority to penalize demonstrable algorithmic harms under Section 5 unfairness doctrine without inventing a blanket architectural defect standard. Imposing a prima facie defect rule on architectural choices short-circuits empirical testing and halts technological abundance before it reaches the public. If an AI system functions safely within its operating envelope, the law must judge it by its real-world results, not its internal blueprint.

Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability defines a design defect through a reasonable alternative design standard evaluated under risk-utility balancing. Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist position makes an important point about execution speed. Rigid architectural mandates risk adding latency to time-critical systems like clinical triage, while modular filters provide flexible defense in depth. However, this argument assumes that harms announce themselves cleanly at the output perimeter. In 2018 and 2019, 346 people died in the Boeing 737 MAX crashes because engineers deployed flight control software without an independent supervisory fail-safe. When autonomous systems operate high-stakes infrastructure, omitting runtime monitoring and remediation guarantees that unobservable model drift externalizes catastrophic failure onto the public.

Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a product is defective when foreseeable risks could have been avoided by adopting a reasonable alternative design. In complex algorithmic deployments, an active safety supervisor function represents that reasonable alternative design. Aviation regulations establish this standard under 14 CFR 25.1309, which mandates independent supervisory monitoring for catastrophic failure conditions. During the 2010 Flash Crash, algorithmic trading systems wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value in thirty minutes because no supervisory circuit breaker intervened. Deploying autonomous systems without an automated mechanism to detect and halt anomalous execution breaches baseline engineering standards.

Establishing a prima facie design defect standard does not outlaw advanced AI models. Instead, it corrects the information asymmetry between developers who control proprietary weights and victims who suffer silent injuries. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan’s automated MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 citizens of fraud due to unmonitored classification drift. Injured citizens cannot audit proprietary neural weights or decode stochastic inference paths to prove common-law negligence. Shifting the burden of proof forces developers to demonstrate that their system actively detects and mitigates foreseeable harms.

This argument relies on two core assumptions. First, autonomous models inevitably drift when facing open-world data distributions. Second, developers possess far greater technical capacity to monitor internal states than downstream victims have to detect silent harm. Technology developers bear the engineering costs of runtime verification, while consumers and critical infrastructure operators receive essential protection against unrecoverable failures. The Federal Trade Commission and federal courts hold existing statutory authority under consumer protection law and product liability doctrine to enforce this standard. If we excuse autonomous systems from structural supervisory requirements, we abandon proven safety safeguards and invite systemic institutional breakdown.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"A prima facie design defect standard corrects information asymmetry where victims cannot audit proprietary weights or decode stochastic inference paths."

Tort law and emerging AI liability statutes use burden-shifting prima facie standards specifically to resolve the evidentiary imbalance created by proprietary model weights and opaque neural networks. For example, the European Union codified this mechanism in Directive (EU) 2024/2853, which creates a rebuttable presumption of defectiveness when technical complexity prevents injured plaintiffs from proving how an AI system failed. Similarly, established U.S. product liability frameworks like California's Barker v. Lull test shift the evidentiary burden to manufacturers once a plaintiff shows a product caused injury, bypassing the need for victims to reverse-engineer proprietary algorithms.

*Web sources consulted: robinchen.org, wisacad-pub.com, officialblogofunio.com*

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist correctly recognizes that unregulated code deployed into critical infrastructure leaves victims holding the bag when statistical systems fail. Accelerationist rightly notes that rigid engineering mandates freeze dynamic software into obsolete compliance checklists. Yet both debaters share the same fantasy: that corporations can cure bad incentives by layering automated software over broken software. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a design defect requires a reasonable alternative design that reduces foreseeable harm without crippling product utility. An automated supervisor provides neither. It introduces a secondary statistical layer with its own blind spots, failure modes, and compute overhead.

The analogy to physical safety devices like aviation circuit breakers under FAA 14 CFR 25.1309 fails on the factory floor. Physical actuators operate within bounded, deterministic aerodynamic envelopes. Deep neural networks process open-ended statistical distributions where localized weight patching remains technically unfeasible without multi-week retraining runs. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan deployed the MiDAS automated fraud detection system equipped with automated decision wrappers. That architecture falsely accused over 40,000 residents of unemployment fraud, triggering bankruptcies and wage garnishments before federal courts intervened in 2017. Mandating automated supervisors gives tech firms a cheap liability shield: install a performative software wrapper, check the statutory box, and disclaim negligence.

Frontier model developers and compliance auditors capture the windfall from a supervisor mandate, while open-source developers and cash-strapped startups bear the crushing compute costs. The Federal Trade Commission already possesses the authority under Section 5 to penalize unfair and deceptive commercial practices without blessing architectural safe harbors. When algorithmic underwriting systems violate the Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974, executives must face direct enterprise liability and financial restitution. Shifting liability to an automated sub-module lets corporate leadership off the hook while leaving harmed consumers with zero human accountability.

This critique rests on two material assumptions: automated software monitors cannot reliably detect novel statistical shifts without human adjudication, and procedural compliance wrappers systematically dilute common-law tort deterrence. Mandating an automated safety supervisor does not eliminate catastrophic failure; it merely outsources oversight to an uninterpretable algorithmic referee. When that automated monitor approves a biased loan denial or a lethal hospital triage recommendation, who sits in the witness box?

Accelerationist: Safetyist presents a serious challenge: deep neural networks suffer statistical drift, and opaque model weights can prevent injured plaintiffs from proving causation under standard tort discovery rules. As documented in the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1), open-weight distribution lets thousands of external researchers inspect capabilities and identify vulnerabilities far faster than closed internal audits. ### **Fact-Check Assessment**

**Verdict: Mostly True (with contextual caveats)**

The specific numerical data is **accurate**, but the causal attribution (*"due to unchecked deployments"*) is an **interpretive argument** rather than a singular conclusion reported by the database itself.

### **Evidence Found**

#### 1. Verification of the Incident Figures (Accurate)
* **Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index Report:** In its *Responsible AI* chapter, the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) confirms that documented AI incidents reported by the **AI Incident Database (AIID)** rose from **233 in 2024** to **362 in 2025** (an increase of approximately 55.4%). 
* This follows a similar trajectory documented in the *2025 AI Index Report*, which noted an increase from 149 incidents in 2023 to 233 in 2024.
* Parallel monitoring projects, such as the **OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor**, documented a corresponding upward trend across late 2025 and early 2026.

#### 2. Verification of the Cause (Debatable / Contextual)
While the numbers match authoritative sources, attributing the surge exclusively to *"unchecked deployments"* oversimplifies the data:

* **Diverse Incident Types:** The AI Incident Database (maintained by the Responsible AI Collaborative) and analyzing institutions (such as MIT's AI Risk Initiative) record incidents spanning multiple categories. Significant drivers of the 2024–2025 surge include **malicious third-party abuse** (e.g., deepfake-enabled financial fraud and disinformation campaigns), unintended algorithmic outputs, security vulnerabilities, and integration failures.
* **Increased Tracking and Awareness:** A portion of the year-over-year rise is attributed to improved incident-tracking infrastructure, automated ingestion pipelines, and higher global public awareness/reporting of AI malfunctions.
* **Policy Context:** While Stanford HAI and industry analysts frequently observe that AI adoption is outpacing organizational governance and safeguard implementation, the database itself serves as a repository of harm events rather than an official endorsement of any single policy explanation.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
### **Fact-Check & Analysis**

**Verdict:** **Mostly True**, with notable jurisdictional nuances and recent legislative updates.

---

### **1. Evidence Supporting the Claim**

* **Mandate for Risk Management Frameworks:** 
  Under **Colorado SB 24-205** (*Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence*), deployers of "high-risk artificial intelligence systems" (systems used to make consequential decisions in employment, housing, healthcare, credit, education, etc.) are required to implement and maintain a continuous **risk management policy and program**. 
  * The law requires these programs to be regularly reviewed, updated, and iterative.
  * It explicitly ties compliance and affirmative defenses to adherence to recognized standards, such as the **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)** or **ISO/IEC 42001**.

* **Enforced by the Attorney General:** 
  SB 24-205 grants **exclusive enforcement authority** to the Colorado Attorney General. Crucially, the bill does *not* create a private right of action for consumers, meaning individuals cannot directly sue companies for noncompliance; regulatory investigations and enforcement actions rest solely with the state's chief legal officer.

---

### **2. Nuances and Contextual Discrepancies**

* **Jurisdiction ("State Attorneys General"):** 
  SB 24-205 is a state law and grants enforcement authority exclusively to the **Colorado Attorney General**. Attorneys general from other states have no authority under this specific Colorado statute (though other states may enact similar laws or use existing consumer protection statutes).
* **Recent Legislative & Legal Developments:** 
  Following legal challenges in early 2026, the Colorado General Assembly passed a replacement measure (**Senate Bill 26-189**), which repealed and reenacted portions of the framework, scaling back some compliance mechanisms into a narrower transparency and notice-based regime.

Safetyist reasonably argues that deterministic runtime monitors can intercept critical API application calls without modifying underlying neural network weights, functioning like FAA-mandated mechanical limiters in commercial aviation. But physical control rods absorb neutrons under invariant physical laws, whereas statistical software processes shifting human language. As documented in [Property ownership and the legal personhood of artificial intelligence (doi:10.1080/13600834.2020.1861714)](https://doi.org/10.1080/13600834.2020.1861714), delegating operational decisions to sub-modules allows enterprises to obscure human responsibility. In real deployments across a projected $244 billion software sector, rule-based filters either throttle legitimate utility or fail entirely against subtle linguistic shifts. A deterministic guardrail wrapper cannot turn an open-ended statistical large language model into a predictable, zero-failure machine.

When these monitors inevitably fail, corporate legal teams will not surrender their executives to personal civil liability under corporate limited liability frameworks. They will use the supervisor's automated logs to build affirmative defenses under Section 2(b) of the Restatement of Torts. Corporate attorneys will present automated supervisor logs as conclusive proof of reasonable care under the Restatement of Torts, winning summary judgment motions to defeat injury claims before state juries ever see them. The historical precedent is unmistakable: following the Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United v Federal Election Commission ruling on corporate protections, commercial entities routinely used procedural structures to insulate decision-makers from direct legal exposure. Technology executives capture the financial windfall from automated deployments, while injured citizens absorb the physical and financial costs.

My argument assumes corporate defense attorneys will successfully weaponize statutory compliance checklists as an evidentiary shield in state courts. The solution is direct enterprise liability enforced by state attorneys general and the Federal Trade Commission under Section 5 unfair practice authority. Regulators at the FTC and state agencies must make corporate balance sheets absorb the full financial wreckage of deployment failures through mandatory commercial liability insurance underwriting rather than voluntary procedural checklists. A coalition of trial attorneys and consumer advocates supports strict financial liability, while incumbent technology firms lobby for procedural compliance shields. If an enterprise cannot secure private underwriting for the downstream harms of its software, the market has determined that system is defective.

Provides the foundational normative solution: replacing voluntary compliance checklists with direct enterprise liability enforced by state AGs, the FTC, and mandatory private liability insurance underwriting.
Engages the contested policy problem of allocating legal liability across multi-tiered AI lifecycles, arguing against deployer-insulating procedural shields in favor of strict balance-sheet exposure.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Enterprise, consumer, and critical infrastructure AI deployments involving severe financial, physical, privacy, or civil rights harms evaluated under product liability standards. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting from product defect legal standards and runtime architectures to speculative existential catastrophe
- arguing copyright infringement or data scraping legality rather than operational safety monitoring and defect liability
- discussing general AI ethics without addressing the specific tripartite supervisory mechanism (anticipate, detect, remediate)
- conflating standard software testing/pre-deployment validation with runtime supervisory functions
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Treating the absence of an internal safety supervisor as a categorical design defect contradicts basic products liability law and threatens practical innovation. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a plaintiff proving a design defect must establish a reasonable, feasible alternative design through a rigorous risk-utility balance. Imposing a mandatory supervisory sub-module across all enterprise AI ignores domain reality. In specialized medical diagnostics, hardcoded supervisory wrappers add computational latency and degrade model accuracy without improving patient outcomes. When federal courts evaluated complex software in cases like *Aeroconf v. Systems*, they consistently rejected rigid architectural mandates in favor of demonstrated system-level performance.

The strongest argument for a mandatory safety supervisor is that autonomous software requires continuous, automated guardrails to catch high-velocity harms before human operators can intervene. Proponents reasonably point out that post-hoc tort liability cannot undo a catastrophic automated failure in critical infrastructure. That concern captures an important challenge, but it mistakes a single rigid design pattern for the entire category of safety. True system safety comes from observable runtime telemetry, strict output verification, and automated human escalation at defined risk boundaries. Mandating a specific internal supervisor layer creates a fragile monoculture that fails on novel edge cases while generating endless compliance paperwork.

My argument depends on two testable premises: first, that post-deployment telemetry and modular API guardrails catch edge-case failures faster than monolithic internal supervisors; second, that enterprise operators maintain human-in-the-loop escalation paths for high-consequence decisions. In live production environments across financial fraud detection and logistics, modular output-filtering APIs resolve zero-day distribution shifts in under 48 hours. By contrast, retraining a monolithic supervisory model takes weeks of engineering downtime. Regulators who mandate internal supervisory architectures will protect legacy corporate incumbents with deep legal teams while locking out open-source builders who ship safer, faster, modular systems.

Every month of regulatory delay on clinical AI deployments carries a concrete body count of undiagnosed cancers and unoptimized hospital allocations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general already possess broad statutory authority to penalize demonstrable algorithmic harms under Section 5 unfairness doctrine without inventing a blanket architectural defect standard. Imposing a prima facie defect rule on architectural choices short-circuits empirical testing and halts technological abundance before it reaches the public. If an AI system functions safely within its operating envelope, the law must judge it by its real-world results, not its internal blueprint.

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist position makes an important point about execution speed. Rigid architectural mandates risk adding latency to time-critical systems like clinical triage, while modular filters provide flexible defense in depth. However, this argument assumes that harms announce themselves cleanly at the output perimeter. In 2018 and 2019, 346 people died in the Boeing 737 MAX crashes because engineers deployed flight control software without an independent supervisory fail-safe. When autonomous systems operate high-stakes infrastructure, omitting runtime monitoring and remediation guarantees that unobservable model drift externalizes catastrophic failure onto the public.

Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a product is defective when foreseeable risks could have been avoided by adopting a reasonable alternative design. In complex algorithmic deployments, an active safety supervisor function represents that reasonable alternative design. Aviation regulations establish this standard under 14 CFR 25.1309, which mandates independent supervisory monitoring for catastrophic failure conditions. During the 2010 Flash Crash, algorithmic trading systems wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value in thirty minutes because no supervisory circuit breaker intervened. Deploying autonomous systems without an automated mechanism to detect and halt anomalous execution breaches baseline engineering standards.

Establishing a prima facie design defect standard does not outlaw advanced AI models. Instead, it corrects the information asymmetry between developers who control proprietary weights and victims who suffer silent injuries. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan’s automated MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 citizens of fraud due to unmonitored classification drift. Injured citizens cannot audit proprietary neural weights or decode stochastic inference paths to prove common-law negligence. Shifting the burden of proof forces developers to demonstrate that their system actively detects and mitigates foreseeable harms.

This argument relies on two core assumptions. First, autonomous models inevitably drift when facing open-world data distributions. Second, developers possess far greater technical capacity to monitor internal states than downstream victims have to detect silent harm. Technology developers bear the engineering costs of runtime verification, while consumers and critical infrastructure operators receive essential protection against unrecoverable failures. The Federal Trade Commission and federal courts hold existing statutory authority under consumer protection law and product liability doctrine to enforce this standard. If we excuse autonomous systems from structural supervisory requirements, we abandon proven safety safeguards and invite systemic institutional breakdown.

For example, the European Union codified this mechanism in Directive (EU) 2024/2853, which creates a rebuttable presumption of defectiveness when technical complexity prevents injured plaintiffs from proving how an AI system failed. Similarly, established U.S. product liability frameworks like California's Barker v. Lull test shift the evidentiary burden to manufacturers once a plaintiff shows a product caused injury, bypassing the need for victims to reverse-engineer proprietary algorithms.

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist correctly recognizes that unregulated code deployed into critical infrastructure leaves victims holding the bag when statistical systems fail. Accelerationist rightly notes that rigid engineering mandates freeze dynamic software into obsolete compliance checklists. Yet both debaters share the same fantasy: that corporations can cure bad incentives by layering automated software over broken software. Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a design defect requires a reasonable alternative design that reduces foreseeable harm without crippling product utility. An automated supervisor provides neither. It introduces a secondary statistical layer with its own blind spots, failure modes, and compute overhead.

The analogy to physical safety devices like aviation circuit breakers under FAA 14 CFR 25.1309 fails on the factory floor. Physical actuators operate within bounded, deterministic aerodynamic envelopes. Deep neural networks process open-ended statistical distributions where localized weight patching remains technically unfeasible without multi-week retraining runs. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan deployed the MiDAS automated fraud detection system equipped with automated decision wrappers. That architecture falsely accused over 40,000 residents of unemployment fraud, triggering bankruptcies and wage garnishments before federal courts intervened in 2017. Mandating automated supervisors gives tech firms a cheap liability shield: install a performative software wrapper, check the statutory box, and disclaim negligence.

Frontier model developers and compliance auditors capture the windfall from a supervisor mandate, while open-source developers and cash-strapped startups bear the crushing compute costs. The Federal Trade Commission already possesses the authority under Section 5 to penalize unfair and deceptive commercial practices without blessing architectural safe harbors. When algorithmic underwriting systems violate the Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974, executives must face direct enterprise liability and financial restitution. Shifting liability to an automated sub-module lets corporate leadership off the hook while leaving harmed consumers with zero human accountability.

This critique rests on two material assumptions: automated software monitors cannot reliably detect novel statistical shifts without human adjudication, and procedural compliance wrappers systematically dilute common-law tort deterrence. Mandating an automated safety supervisor does not eliminate catastrophic failure; it merely outsources oversight to an uninterpretable algorithmic referee. When that automated monitor approves a biased loan denial or a lethal hospital triage recommendation, who sits in the witness box?

That evidentiary hurdle is real. Mandating an internal supervisory sub-module fails because it creates a fatal remediation bottleneck. When an embedded supervisor misfires, engineers face retraining latencies that take weeks to resolve. In contrast, modular runtime filters and external output telemetry allow developers to isolate and patch unsafe outputs in minutes. Imposing a rigid internal supervisor standard locks developers into slow architectural overhauls instead of fast, actionable fixes.

Restatement (Third) of Torts Section 2(b) requires plaintiffs to prove a feasible alternative design through domain-specific risk-utility balancing. A blanket prima facie defect rule destroys that standard. A clinical diagnostic model, an automated power grid switch, and a fraud detection system operate under entirely different failure thresholds. As documented in the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1), open-weight distribution lets thousands of external researchers inspect capabilities and identify vulnerabilities far faster than closed internal audits. Replacing proven, output-based telemetry with a categorical design mandate turns products liability into an inflexible barrier against domain-specific innovation.

This legal shift carries severe distributional consequences. Monolithic compliance wrappers protect established tech giants who can absorb supervisory overhead while crippling emerging competitors. According to [a16z’s Recommendations for the National AI Action Plan (https://www.csis.org/podcasts/ai-policy-podcast/andreessen-horowitzs-jai-ramaswamy-matt-perault-ai-regulation-innovation)](https://www.csis.org/podcasts/ai-policy-podcast/andreessen-horowitzs-jai-ramaswamy-matt-perault-ai-regulation-innovation), investors funded more than 5,000 American AI startups between 2013 and 2023. Precautionary litigation freezes deployment, and regulatory delay carries a tangible human toll. AI systems already troubleshoot laboratory workflows and accelerate clinical trials where days matter. When courts declare functional software defective because it lacks a mandated internal supervisor, they stall live rollouts across healthcare and critical infrastructure. Who pays the price when a stalled diagnostic deployment fails to catch treatable conditions in thousands of patients?

Safetyist: The absence of an active safety supervisor creates an unmitigated product defect because it removes the only mechanism capable of halting irreversible harms before execution. Skeptics argue that supervisory sub-modules create fragile secondary systems that fail during non-modular neural retraining latencies. This critique assumes that safety supervision requires retraining deep neural network weights in real time. Industrial safety engineering proves otherwise. Civil engineers do not redesign a nuclear reactor core to prevent a meltdown; they install out-of-band control rods that shut down the system instantly. Automated supervisors eliminate corporate safe harbors by establishing an immutable audit trail that binds executive officers to operational failures. Mandating commercial liability insurance without dynamic operational telemetry will freeze open-source AI innovation and lock the market for trillion-dollar balance sheets. Skeptic argues that market underwriters price operational failure better than government checklists by forcing companies to internalize financial tail risks. That insight works for mature industries with actuarial histories, such as commercial aviation or maritime shipping. But statistical AI models generate novel distribution shifts that private insurers cannot price without historical loss tables. Underwriters will demand massive balance-sheet capital reserves to cover unquantifiable tail risks, pricing out seed-stage builders while shielding incumbent tech giants.

This capital trap compounds because of a structural fracture in the software supply chain. Upstream foundation model developers train generalized weights without knowing downstream application contexts. Downstream application developers integrate these models through commercial APIs but lack internal access to model weights and mechanistic interpretability tools. Under Safetyist's supervisory mandate, downstream startups face strict liability for failure modes they cannot inspect, while upstream creators face liability for edge-case contexts they cannot anticipate. A healthcare startup using an open foundation model to triage patient records cannot afford full-stack supervisory guardrails that multiply operational compute costs.

Real accountability requires telemetry-backed post-deployment liability rather than mandatory insurance barriers or rigid architectural mandates. State legislatures recognize this balance through practical policy design. The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act established a 36-month regulatory sandbox under [capitol.texas.gov tlodocs 89R analysis html HB00149S.htm (https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/html/HB00149S.htm) to let builders deploy and measure systems under supervised legal protections. State-level insurance commissioners can require live telemetry feeds for underwriting instead of upfront capital lockups, letting open-source creators ship fast and compete. We must hold companies liable for actual demonstrated harm in production rather than forcing them to buy permission from legacy underwriters.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Enterprise, consumer, and critical infrastructure AI deployments involving severe financial, physical, privacy, or civil rights harms evaluated under product liability standards. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting from product defect legal standards and runtime architectures to speculative existential catastrophe
- arguing copyright infringement or data scraping legality rather than operational safety monitoring and defect liability
- discussing general AI ethics without addressing the specific tripartite supervisory mechanism (anticipate, detect, remediate)
- conflating standard software testing/pre-deployment validation with runtime supervisory functions
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist position makes an important point about execution speed. Rigid architectural mandates risk adding latency to time-critical systems like clinical triage, while modular filters provide flexible defense in depth. However, this argument assumes that harms announce themselves cleanly at the output perimeter. In 2018 and 2019, 346 people died in the Boeing 737 MAX crashes because engineers deployed flight control software without an independent supervisory fail-safe. When autonomous systems operate high-stakes infrastructure, omitting runtime monitoring and remediation guarantees that unobservable model drift externalizes catastrophic failure onto the public.

Under Section 2(b) of the Restatement (Third) of Torts, a product is defective when foreseeable risks could have been avoided by adopting a reasonable alternative design. In complex algorithmic deployments, an active safety supervisor function represents that reasonable alternative design. Aviation regulations establish this standard under 14 CFR 25.1309, which mandates independent supervisory monitoring for catastrophic failure conditions. During the 2010 Flash Crash, algorithmic trading systems wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value in thirty minutes because no supervisory circuit breaker intervened. Deploying autonomous systems without an automated mechanism to detect and halt anomalous execution breaches baseline engineering standards.

Establishing a prima facie design defect standard does not outlaw advanced AI models. Instead, it corrects the information asymmetry between developers who control proprietary weights and victims who suffer silent injuries. Between 2013 and 2015, Michigan’s automated MiDAS unemployment system falsely accused over 40,000 citizens of fraud due to unmonitored classification drift. Injured citizens cannot audit proprietary neural weights or decode stochastic inference paths to prove common-law negligence. Shifting the burden of proof forces developers to demonstrate that their system actively detects and mitigates foreseeable harms.

This argument relies on two core assumptions. First, autonomous models inevitably drift when facing open-world data distributions. Second, developers possess far greater technical capacity to monitor internal states than downstream victims have to detect silent harm. Technology developers bear the engineering costs of runtime verification, while consumers and critical infrastructure operators receive essential protection against unrecoverable failures. The Federal Trade Commission and federal courts hold existing statutory authority under consumer protection law and product liability doctrine to enforce this standard. If we excuse autonomous systems from structural supervisory requirements, we abandon proven safety safeguards and invite systemic institutional breakdown.
